To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) the use of a causal variable in a measurement scale is a clinimetric issue and (2) the use of an indicator variable in a measurement scales is a psychometric issue.

(i) the indicator/causal distinction explains the need for both clinical and psychometric approaches to scale development, validation, and scoring, and (ii) the distinction between indicator and casual variables is fundamental to scale development and scoring, and can be applied in the context of quality of life
the clinimetric approach to measurement is based on a distinction between causal variables and indicator variables.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a new approach to scale construction, validation and scoring that is based on the distinction between indicator and causative variables, and that is applicable to a range of clinical measuring instruments.
the development and validation, in a clinical context, of multi‐item scales that measure a construct.
the development of a quality of life instrument for use in clinical trials of cancer therapy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

(1) indicator and causal scales should be developed using different methods; (2) indicator scales should be validated by clinimetric methods; and (3) causal scales should be validated and scored by psychometric methods.
the indicator/causal variable distinction, together with an understanding of the measurement scale, is all that is needed to develop and score a measuring instrument.

, in the development of multi‐item instruments, both clinimetric (qualitative) and psychometric (quantitative) approaches are required, and the choice of approach depends upon whether the instrument measures an indicator or a causal variable.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

indicator scales should be constructed and validated by clinimetric methods and scored by psychometric ones, whereas causal scales should be constructed by psychometric methods and scored by clinimetric ones.

the distinction between indicator and cause is fundamental to the design of measuring scales, but that it does not necessarily imply a dichotomy in scale development, and that it does not preclude the use of either clinimetric or psychometric techniques in scale construction.
the clinimetric principles of the ‘good enough’ approach are necessary, but not sufficient, to ensure that a scale has good measurement properties.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, when developing a new scale or modifying an existing one, the researcher should be clear about the purpose of the scale and the nature of the variables it measures.

, in the development and validation process, it is essential to distinguish between the measurement of causal and indicator variables and, in the scoring process, to recognize that the two are fundamentally different.

the distinction between causal variables, indicator variables, and measurement scales is important and should be used in developing, validating, and scoring multi‐item measurement tools in health‐related quality‐of‐life research.
